topic: The left-digit effect: why $9.99 feels much cheaper than $10
title: Why $9.99 Looks Cheaper Than $10
voiceover: Why does $9.99 feel so much cheaper than $10? Researchers call it the left-digit effect. In five experiments, Manoj Thomas and Vicki Morwitz found that a nine-ending price looks smaller than a price one cent higher. But only when the leftmost digits differ, like $2.99 versus $3.00. They also found the effect was stronger when the two prices being compared were close together. And it appeared with other multi-digit numbers, not just prices. A separate analysis found that firms tend to use more round prices for higher-quality products. Researcher Mark Stiving argued that firms signaling quality are more likely to use round prices. So when a price ends in nine, try rounding it up to the next number before you decide. Tomorrow: why do you test only the ideas you already believe?

New psychology short every day on The Psyche Discourse. Source: Thomas, M., & Morwitz, V. G. (2005). Penny wise and pound foolish: The left-digit effect in price cognition. Journal of Consumer Research, 32(1), 54-64. Source: Stiving, M. (2000). Price-endings when prices signal quality. Management Science, 46(12), 1617-1629.
accuracy_note: Thomas & Morwitz (2005) identify when the effect occurs; its size varies. Stiving (2000) is an economic model plus empirical evidence that firms use round prices more for higher-quality products; the model is debated (a 2003 comment exists).
